name: North Branch Bridge
aka: the first bridge over the North Branch

documented_range.note: THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED BY A YEAR AND THE DISPUTE DOES NOT REACH THE SCENE. Andreas: 'In the summer of 1832 Samuel Miller ... built the first bridge over the North Branch.' Charles Cleaver, recalled in 1893, gives the winter of 1831-32. Summer 1832 is adopted, on the ground that Cleaver did not reach Chicago until October 1833 — so his date is hearsay reported sixty years later, while Andreas's is a compiler's date from the 1880s working over the town's own records. Either way the bridge stood well before 1835-07-01 and this record models one phase. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE ONLY ONE THIS PROJECT HAS THAT IS ACTUALLY ATTESTED: the Kinzie Street chronology closes bridge #1 in 1839, superseded by a pontoon swing. That is a table's summary rather than Andreas's prose, so the range carries the same inferred tag as its opening. What the range does NOT claim is that the structure was unchanged across it — see the form notes: a bridge described as useless for teams in 1833 carried a large procession in August 1835, and nothing reached records what happened in between.

position.symbolic_location: Across the North Branch on the Kinzie Street alignment, its west landing near the south-east corner of Kinzie and Canal Streets.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-10, AND THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED WHERE THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the same rule the Green Tree's placement uses. Andreas locates the bridge 'near the southeast corner of Kinzie and Canal streets, in the vicinity of the present bridge of the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Company'; the war-dance account of 18 August 1835 corroborates the line by having a procession cross the North Branch bridge and then turn south along West Water Street in front of the Green Tree and Wolf Point taverns. Method: the modern Kinzie and Canal intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (three shared nodes, mean 41.889068 N, -87.640156 W = EPSG:26916 E 446891.7, N 4637657.8, local N +262.0), and Kinzie Street is one of the streets that survives on its 1835 alignment. The DECK CENTRELINE is set on that northing and its ends are set where the traced 1834 waterline crosses it — not where the modern banks are, because the modern channel is a dredged and walled successor and using it would put the abutments on nineteenth-century engineering. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin, which is the deck's south-west corner (west end, upstream side), per docs/GLB-CONTRACT.md. Facade bearing 0: this archetype's convention is that a deck at rotation 0 runs east-west with its upstream side north, and the Kinzie alignment runs east-west. WHAT THE CORNER DOES NOT SAY: modern Canal Street at this northing lies 63 m WEST of the traced 1834 west bank, so 'the south-east corner of Kinzie and Canal' is where the approach began and not where the bridge did. That gap is a fact about the two streets, not an error bar. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus the trace's own; along the street the position is better constrained than across it, because the crossing has to meet both banks.

footprint.note: THE DECK OUTLINE, AND THE ONLY FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS NOT A PLACEHOLDER — both of its dimensions come from something. The width, 3.048 m, is Cleaver's 'These bridges were ten feet wide', recorded here in its original unit. The length, 71.83 m, is MEASURED rather than chosen: it is the distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Kinzie alignment, read off data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson at the crossing station (west bank local E -117.52, east bank local E -45.69), which is the same Wright 1834 segmentation the ground and the river are built from. It agrees with the reach's drafted mean width of 72.9 m to about a metre. THE SPAN IS THEREFORE AN OVERSTATEMENT OF THE CLEAR SPAN, deliberately and by an unrecorded amount: Cleaver puts the abutments 'in the shallow water near the banks', which is inside the drawn line, and nobody recorded how far inside. Landing the deck exactly on the traced waterline was chosen because that line is the one thing here that is evidence — the terrain surface crosses Z=0 along it by construction — and an inset would have added a second invention on top of the first. Carried uncertainty: the georeference's plus or minus 20 m, which is larger than the difference being argued about.

construction.note: Andreas: 'It was formed of stringers.' Cleaver: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs.' Two independent accounts, both describing round or hewn timber rather than framed carpentry, which is what this archetype's 'log' value means.

width_m.note: TEN FEET, from Charles Cleaver, of both branch bridges. This is the only dimension of any structure in this dataset that a source actually states, and it is worth saying why it is trusted at tier 2: Cleaver was recalling a bridge he had used and had driven a team across, and a width is the kind of number a user of a narrow bridge remembers. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding.

clearance_m.note: SIX FEET ABOVE THE WATER — AND THIS RECORD DOWNGRADES THE FIGURE, which is the correction it carries. The project's crossings dossier, docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 5, gives both branch bridges as 'about 10 ft wide, clearing the water by about 6 ft' and tags the pair as documented. The width is documented and now has its source; the clearance does not. Searching the transcriptions that carry the rest of this bridge's evidence returns the width, the log abutments, the stringers and the 1832 date, and nothing anywhere about a height above the water. The number is kept because it is the dossier's and because it is plausible for a stringer bridge crossing shallow water with cribbed abutments, but it is recorded as INFERRED until the page behind it is found. See docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md. The archetype's DOC_CLEARANCE_M constant carried the same overstatement and its docstring is corrected in the same slice.

abutments.note: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs in the shallow water near the banks.' The one structural statement anybody made about these bridges, and it is specific: the ends were carried on log cribs standing OUT IN THE WATER rather than on dry-land bearings.

pier_kind.note: A DISAGREEMENT PICKED WITH REASONING RATHER THAN SILENTLY. Cleaver describes heavy logs standing in shallow water, which is a crib — a log box, sunk and filled. The Kinzie Street page's chronology table instead types the bridge 'Wood, Fixed, Bent', and a bent is framed and usually pile-borne. Crib is adopted because Cleaver is an eyewitness describing what he saw and the table is a modern editorial classification applied uniformly down a column covering six bridges and a century. THE INFERENCE IS THE STEP FROM ABUTMENTS TO PIERS, not the choice between the two words: Cleaver describes the ends, nobody describes the middle, and this record assumes the intermediate supports were built the way the ends were.

pier_spacing_m.note: NOT ATTESTED IN ANY FORM. Nothing reached says how many supports this bridge had, how far apart they stood, or whether it had any at all between its abutments. It must have had some — 71.83 m is far beyond any log stringer — but the number is the archetype's default, retained deliberately rather than replaced by a fresh guess, and it sets the bay count at 16 and therefore puts 15 cribs in the river. That is the most conspicuous invention in this structure: a visitor sees a row of supports marching across the water and nothing in the record says there was a row. Stated on the record instead of left to default silently, which is the lesson docs/LIBERTIES.md L24 was written for, and admitted in L29.

stringer_count.note: THE 1835 READING OF A BRIDGE THAT CHANGED. Andreas describes the 1832 structure as 'formed of stringers and only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' even in the summer of 1833; six and a half weeks after this scene's date a procession of hundreds crossed it, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. Something was rebuilt or widened between 1833 and 1835 and no source reached says what. Four stringers under a full-width deck is the later, load-carrying reading, chosen because the scene date is 1835-07-01 and the evidence for 1835 is a crowd on the deck. The alternative — the 1832 walkway, two stringers and a plank — is a defensible model of a different year and would be the right value in an 1833 scene.

railing.note: NO RAILING, AND THE ABSENCE IS A CLAIM, so it is stated rather than defaulted. No source reached mentions a railing on either branch bridge; the descriptions that exist run the other way, toward a causeway of logs rather than a piece of engineering. A railed deck reads to a visitor as considered infrastructure and an unrailed one reads as a plank over water, so adding one to look finished would change what the scene says about how developed the town was. The counter-argument is on the record in generators/archetypes/bridge_timber.py: a procession of hundreds crossing an unrailed deck nearly two metres above water is an alarming picture, and that is an argument about the 1835 rebuild rather than evidence about a railing.

ground_contact.note: THE BRIDGE ARRIVES NOWHERE, AND NOTHING IN THIS RECORD IS WRONG. The deck stands 2.22 m above the design water surface — Cleaver's clearance plus the stringer and plank depth the archetype builds under it — while the modelled ground at both landings is the traced 1834 waterline, which is Z = 0 by construction, and the highest land anywhere in the 640 m terrain box reaches only 1.31 m. So the deck ends 2.42 m above the ground beneath them and no ground in this epoch rises to meet them. What is missing is the APPROACH at either end, and it is missing because nothing describes it: Andreas gives the stringers, Cleaver gives the width and the log abutments 'in the shallow water near the banks', and no source reached says how a person or a team got from the bank up onto the deck — an embankment, a trestle ramp, a sloping run of the deck itself, or a lower bridge than the dossier's unsourced six feet. Building one would be a second invention stacked on the clearance figure, which is itself only inferred, and it would be the invention a visitor walks over. It is left out and declared instead. What would settle it: a period depiction of the crossing, or a levelled section — the 1834/1835 Wabansia and Kinzie's Addition plat is the best candidate. Admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md L30.

phases.change_note: The single phase this structure has: a log stringer bridge on cribbed abutments, carrying the Kinzie Street line across the North Branch. The 1832 walkway and whatever it became by 1835 are modelled as one phase because no source dates the change; the form attributes take the 1835 reading and say so.

function.note: A public crossing, and the town's first bridge of any kind — it replaced the Miller-Clybourn ferry that had run across the same water between Miller's house and the Wolf Point Tavern since 1829. By the scene date it is the link between the West Division's Canal Street frontage and the north bank.

research_note: THE FIRST BRIDGE IN CHICAGO, and the first structure in this dataset that is not a building. It is also the first record here whose dimensions come from evidence rather than from a placeholder: ten feet wide is Charles Cleaver's, and the 71.83 m span is measured off the traced 1834 waterline at the Kinzie Street alignment rather than guessed. THREE DISAGREEMENTS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN RESOLVED AWAY. The build date: Andreas says summer 1832 and Cleaver says winter 1831-32, and Cleaver was not in Chicago until October 1833, so Andreas is adopted. The capacity: Andreas has it 'only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' as late as the summer of 1833, while Cleaver 'remembered driving across the first bridge over the North Branch' and a procession of hundreds crossed it on 18 August 1835 — so it was rebuilt or widened in between and nothing says when or how; the form attributes take the 1835 reading. The pier type: an eyewitness describing heavy logs in shallow water against a modern table's type-word 'Bent'. WHAT THIS RECORD CORRECTS IN THE PROJECT'S OWN RESEARCH: the crossings dossier tags both the width and the six-foot clearance as documented, and only the width could be traced to a source. The clearance is recorded as inferred here and the archetype's docstring is corrected to match. See docs/RESEARCH/north_branch_bridge.md.
